title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. The preregistered design used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer under shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). We executed N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) with deterministic task generation and deterministic validation. Confirmatory, artifact‑grounded outcomes are exact and reproducible: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Execution and reconciliation artifacts show the design produced a deterministic ceiling: shared_initial_generation combined with reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime blocking and scoring prevented the guard from having any opportunity to alter outcomes. We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded results and diagnostics, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations (independent per‑condition generation; distinct post‑hoc scorer; controlled adversarial seeding; difficulty‑stratified sampling; instrumented mitigation metrics) to harden future benchmarks so they can expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and to orchestrate staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work demonstrates feasibility of LLMs producing syntactically plausible templates for configuration and IaC tasks; complementary work shows deterministic verifiers can detect many classes of configuration errors offline. However, the end‑to‑end operational safety question remains: when an LLM generator is paired with runtime verification, does the closed‑loop pipeline produce measurably safer deploy outcomes than an LLM alone? This study evaluates that question under a compact, action‑aware staging benchmark.

Research question and design overview. Under the ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 semantics used here, we ask: does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? We preregistered a paired binary confirmatory design with exactly N=400 paired tasks; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The execution adapter routed one shared LLM candidate per task to both conditions (shared_initial_generation=true) to isolate the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs and to conserve model calls. The chosen generator was gpt‑5‑mini and the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation.
sections.related_work: Prior studies span three related areas that motivated our benchmark and hardening recommendations. First, intent→configuration translation: multiple prototype systems and datasets show LLMs can map natural‑language intent to configuration artifacts, establishing feasibility but also highlighting dataset and generalization limits (representative: intent‑to‑configuration evaluations and PreConfig). Second, verifier‑guided workflows and deterministic verification: work in IaC and network verification demonstrates that verifiers—when sufficiently expressive—catch many syntactic and semantic errors offline; verifier‑guided fine‑tuning and generate–validate–repair loops yield gains in IaC contexts (e.g., TerraFormer and related studies), but closed‑loop runtime integration with agentic pipelines is less explored. Third, agentic and tool‑augmented architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestration) broaden AIOps capabilities while introducing failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, overconfidence) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys and evaluation‑gap reviews repeatedly call for action‑aware benchmarks combining generation, runtime blocking, staged rollout, repair, rollback, and provenance; our action‑aware staging benchmark operationalizes these components and empirically exposes a concrete construct validity pitfall for paired designs when generation variance is intentionally suppressed and scoring is deterministic and shared.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1) as a single primary confirmatory hypothesis (H1) comparing paired safe‑deploy rates (guarded − baseline) across N=400 paired tasks. The primary confirmatory procedure was a permutation‑based paired difference test; prespecified corroborative tests included exact McNemar (two‑sided) and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs. Secondary prespecified outcomes included bootstrap CIs for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts.

Execution contract and critical design choices. We executed the registered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 used both as the runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer. The preregistration explicitly set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task we performed a single model generation and delivered that identical candidate to both baseline and guarded episodes. This reduced model_calls_used to 400 for the 800 planned episodes (model call budget saved versus independent generation). The adapter allowed up to one repair call in the guarded episode; recorded repair_applied flags were false across all episodes. Task generation used a seed‑controlled deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 producing per‑task difficulty metadata (fields such as changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Deterministic replay checks were applied to all agent+simulator pairs as prespecified and passed for every pair.

Operational measurements and scoring. Safe‑deploy outcomes were recorded as binary endpoint decisions from deterministic_netops_validator_v5 using full intent‑constraint validation. The validator produced structured traces (validation_before/after, final_configuration, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, valid flag, violation_count, repair_applied, and timestamps). All execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest, provider call audit, task manifest with per‑task difficulty labels, validator traces, raw responses, and analysis logs) were archived and used without human adjudication in the reported confirmatory analysis.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0. Model calls used = 400 (one shared generation per task); maximum_model_calls = 800 per preregistration. Deterministic replay checks passed for all pairs and no exclusions were recorded.

Confirmatory, artifact‑grounded outcomes. Analysis artifacts record: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table entry is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, giving an observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI is [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numerical values are reproduced directly from the archived analysis outputs.

Repair, rollback, and difficulty aggregation. Across all 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator traces show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. The archived task manifest reports the difficulty distribution used in the run: medium: 80 tasks (20.0%); hard: 160 tasks (40.0%); very_hard: 160 tasks (40.0%). Provider and reconciliation diagnostics recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 400, cache_miss_count = 400, stage_counts: {shared_initial_generation: 400}, condition_counts: {shared: 400}. Deterministic reconciliation checks confirmed pair and episode accounting consistency.
sections.discussion:
Construct‑validity diagnosis: why the design produced a deterministic ceiling. Two preregistered choices together forced concordant outcomes across conditions. First, shared_initial_generation removed within‑pair generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to both baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When that deterministic validator accepts a shared candidate, both conditions necessarily record safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference is mathematically forced to zero. Provider_call_audit evidence (hosted_model_call_event_count = 400; stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 400; condition_counts.shared = 400) documents that every pair used a single shared generation and that no cross‑condition model call variation occurred. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design: it demonstrates the validator’s behavior on identical candidates but does not probe generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics.

Implications for inference and power. The confirmatory statistics (permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; bootstrap CI collapsed to a point at zero) correctly reflect the observed data and the preregistered analysis plan. They do not, however, provide information about the potential value of runtime verification in settings where generator variance exists or where scorers differ between runtime and measurement. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline failure rates; that assumption was falsified here by the particular frozen generator+validator pairing and the shared generation semantics, which invalidates the original power rationale for detecting generator×guard interactions in this run.

Concrete artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations. To preserve opportunities for runtime guards to accept, block, or request repair—and thus to make the primary estimand informative—future preregistered runs should avoid conflating generator variance and scorer invariance. Each recommendation below is implementable using artifacts already present in the archive (task manifest difficulty labels, validator traces with repair_applied and timestamps, and provider_call_audit logs).

1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true). Allow each condition to draw its own LLM candidate per task so the guard has an opportunity to accept or block differing outputs. The execution manifest shows model_calls_used = 400 under shared generation; switching to independent generation would use up to 800 model calls but restores within‑pair stochastic variation needed to measure guard utility.

2) Distinct post‑hoc scorer or held‑out adjudicator. Use a separate implementation (or a randomized/stochastic variant) for post‑hoc scoring to avoid conflating runtime blocking and measurement. Treat runtime guard traces (used for blocking) as operational decisions and use an independent scorer to estimate the same construct for confirmatory inference.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding. Use focused seed perturbations to inject tasks that increase baseline failure rates (guaranteeing nontrivial discordant outcomes). The archived deterministic task generator already includes per‑task difficulty metadata; targeted selection or seeded task variants can ensure a nonzero baseline failure probability without relying on opaque model adversarialization.

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling. Prespecify strata (medium/hard/very_hard) and allocate a confirmatory sample ensuring sufficient representation of 'very_hard' tasks. The archived task manifest records per‑task difficulty labels (current aggregation: medium 80, hard 160, very_hard 160) enabling deterministic stratified resampling in future runs.

5) Instrumented mitigation metrics. Record and preregister numeric mitigation outcomes (repair_attempts, repairs_applied, time‑to‑rollback) as primary or secondary endpoints. Validator traces already include repair_applied flags and validation timestamps; these fields can be promoted to confirmatory outcomes to measure partial mitigation activity even when endpoint concordance is high.

Operational guidance for implementing hardening steps using archived artifacts. The task manifest provides deterministic generation seeds and difficulty labels that enable stratified resampling or targeted adversarial seeding. Validator traces include repair_applied and per‑episode validation timestamps to compute time‑to‑rollback distributions. Provider_call_audit logs show model call accounting and stage semantics and therefore permit verification that independent generation semantics were actually applied (e.g., expected hosted_model_call_event_count would increase toward 800 under independent generation). Prespecifying these changes in a new preregistration will preserve deterministic reproducibility while restoring the statistical signal needed to test generator×guard interactions.

Threats to validity and limitations. Internal validity in this run is reduced by shared generation and reuse of a single deterministic validator for runtime blocking and scoring. Construct validity is limited because deterministic_netops_validator_v5 approximates production checks but omits telemetry noise, asynchronous state, and stochastic adjudication policies. External validity is limited by use of a single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across model, validator, or production heterogeneity. Adversarial robustness was not exercised in this run and remains an open empirical question.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling is a design artifact caused by identical per‑pair generation and reuse of a deterministic validator for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring; it renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here—independent generation per condition, distinct scorer, controlled adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification, and instrumented mitigation metrics—provide concrete, implementable steps (using the archived task manifest and validator traces) to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility. Future preregistered runs that implement these hardening steps can meaningfully exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors and restore inferential relevance for the primary estimand.

disclosure_statement: Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini. Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1. The immutable initial master prompt is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but none were applied (repair_applied = false). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle and were used without manual adjudication.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in the task manifest and can be aggregated by auditors; Table 1 reports the artifact‑extracted aggregated counts and percentages.
